newsitem.title: USA: AWAY ON BUSINESS - Keep that picture handy.
newsitem.headline: AWAY ON BUSINESS - Keep that picture handy.

text.p: Airport security precautions that have been tightened and enforced rigorously since the July 17 explosion of TWA flight 800 may eventually be eased.
That should be good news for business travelers now faced with unpacking, deploying and turning on their laptop computers enroute to the gate.
But one aspect of the current requirements -- that travelers produce a photo ID at check-in -- may well become permanent.
"I think it's about time the airlines in this country knew who actually was flying on their planes," a Florida travel agent wrote in a letter published recently in Travel Weekly magazine.

"Working in the travel business for more than 10 years, I have seen cases where large companies have the entire sales force flying under one person's name (the owner's) so that one person can rack up all the frequent flyer mileage," he added.
"I have never understood how airlines, complaining about not making a profit, could let such a blatant theft occur daily," he said.

The Federal Aviation Administration in tightening the security requirement that travelers present a government-issued photo ID, such as a driver's license, at check-in. There are variations among carriers as to what else an airline may demand, and how they treat someone who does not have a picture ID.
Marlene Kowalsky of St. Clair Travel in O'Fallon, Ill., says travelers have adapted to the requirement very well. She can also see why airlines like the idea.
Travelling under someone else's name for mileage credit or some other reason "is unethical and not a good idea," she said. "I could see this solving some of those problems for the airlines."
She also said that if one of her clients was about to take a trip but had no photo ID, she would intervene with the carrier ahead of time to make sure there would be no check-in problem.

Tom Parsons, author of new book called "Insider Travel Secrets," told the Chicago Tribune recently that the photo ID requirement will stay in place "no matter what. The airlines appreciate the requirement because they are catching a lot of people flying on other people's tickets."

Dennis Marzella, senior vice president for research and strategic marketing at Yesawich, Pepperdine & Brown, an advertising and marketing firm heavily involved in the travel industry, says security concerns have historically been cyclical, ebbing and flowing with various high-profile incidents.
There is nothing to suggest that the stiffest requirements now in place will stay, he said.
The photo ID requirement is a minimal step, he added, but "if someone has a diabolical plan, they'll probably have a ticket and a photo ID to match. It probably does screen out some oddballs though."

On another front, Consumer Reports Travel Letter has done air travelers a service in a report, flush with detail, on the number of toilets per passenger available on various aircraft flown by various airlines.

The publication's September issue reports that on average, there is one lavatory for every 46 passengers in coach, compared with one for 20 business class passengers and one for 11 passengers in first class.
But the numbers vary by airline and make of aircraft, since carriers configure their interiors differently. More seats mean fewer comfort stations.
The four worst planes, and the number of passengers per restroom, it said, "are 737s as outfitted by Continental (90), Delta (95), United (101) and USAir (102).

"Near the bottom of the bowl with ratios of 78-90 are some Aeromexico DC9s and Continental DC10s (90), Air Canada DC9s and some Continental 757s (80), United 757s (82) and Delta and other Continental 757s," tied at 78, it said.
Information on the Travel Letter can be obtained at 1-800-234-1970.
